questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]={e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Notice that for each vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
${e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}].$

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =-3,\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-3t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x\text{-axis}.$ Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector $v=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $w=[0,\text{ }1]^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

The general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{{field-1}}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{2t}{{field-2}}+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{2t}\to $ 
{{field-4}} 
as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach 
{{field-5}}  
as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/c993f6fc9eb12c0d8f60c420519a7db4a5cf78da9f0c24d0ade87b0a96590f59.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ t+1\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=2,$ we get the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x={{field-6}} \\ y=2(t+1){e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.2$ |

| $x$ | $-0.37$ | $0$ | {{field-7}} |

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/9e78fbd54f2825d28581b8181cab7762b7a625f7b21620eec37436771c9e1695.png)
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =2,\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/c993f6fc9eb12c0d8f60c420519a7db4a5cf78da9f0c24d0ade87b0a96590f59.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ t+1\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=2,$ we get the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2t{e}^{2t} \\ y=2(t+1){e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.37$ | $0$ | $0.60$ |
| $y$ | $0.37$ | $2$ | $3.58$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/4232a3293f2414f6121c834fa09145f5f3b573d83ad7a3695c6ca93c228c8563.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/9e78fbd54f2825d28581b8181cab7762b7a625f7b21620eec37436771c9e1695.png)

questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. Select the correct options below regarding the given system.

$\,$ The equilibrium point (origin) is a 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
node.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix of our system is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that:

- Since the only (repeated) eigenvalue of $A$ is $\lambda =3$ and it's positive, we have a $\text{unstable}$ node.

- Since $A$ is diagonal and has a repeated eigenvalue, there are infinitely many linearly independent eigenvectors. So, we have a $\text{star}$ node.

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying the Phase Portrait of a Decoupled System With Repeated Eigenvalues
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-8x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-8y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Sketch the phase portrait of the linear system above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/737c96109e65d59f4df2c2fa574737fe604483fe4ccc9772a3d2bf22ee32e55a.svg)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/22dbda7d3b169206071e5af49fd1fe1af28d86ef1e0a8b37d58eacb62b44c1d2.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=-8$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/5bd691bbaa9542184d90e55aeb16f4dfcd3d22d092b4652e8bddba7bf0b926aa.svg)

The general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/8b25789fb45234e4299e4b5ce3371c1afafc181c64f9802d212ae7cbefc0970f.svg)

Notice that for each vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/674212f0d815e0588faaf276bd797e9822ac5659e5d4b15a7635d7f1327d5dc5.svg) we get the straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/d4c31285e6f31a229bc6fc5cbe2d78e2bf50f73bb6305d91687c5dcc31c3885a.svg)
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/268764bbe776b03647daac7fc77e8ed24107e1bb0cf16d955f7a845a12c65755.svg)

Since $e^{-8t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty,$ so the origin is a stable node.

The phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/4c337f7f6b80f340859844e8217525db98230660d22e760c70218f0c282d21e9.png)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a Decoupled System With Repeated Eigenvalues

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying the Phase Portrait of a System With Repeated Eigenvalues
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector $\mathbf{v} = [1, \ -1]^T$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $\mathbf{w} = [0, \ 1]^T$ is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ Sketch the phase portrait of the linear system above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/72cfb513575d6481a4ee3206ff4d74568dc8397e10fec34ae89242a444a6b2d2.svg) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ -t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/461a22d18752e55eada19b3f0bb58be61bee7a9cd88437304f291c4a9992bdae.svg) has the equation 

$$
y= -x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/ed2fb464c555b2cbf0ffa7f67084e5565fc7c9e80e0263647e1303f69a91895d.svg)
lie on that line. 

Since $e^{-2t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/523dccf73169d02b6bdf4297e96ec84bcc6c43213cdd722000f3a987a534b218.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/0589d1749aed66b91a94b49e4a8815bc4a8621eef3b45e535d2117e81d4f416d.svg)
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{-2t} \\ y=(-t+1){e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-1.36$ | $0$ | $0.18$ |
| $y$ | $4.08$ | $1$ | $0.18$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/dbf5a13ecd5e81c399204fd29d235e410fcb62274555cf3e5b32a383c1078d24.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/6c84cd04f3b037bee48d02d3183114e2668fbbd110bd44e9311e7ff454db8bac.png)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a System With Repeated Eigenvalues

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Classifying Systems of Linear Differential Equations With Repeated Eigenvalues
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above, where the system's matrix has repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=5$ of multiplicity two. Determine the type and stability of the equilibrium point for this linear system.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The matrix of our system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/dda3aceadd2c3bc3b53422d9533f3b5926906de522137d2e0edc4794d658b1fd.svg)

Notice that:

- Since the only (repeated) eigenvalue of $A$ is positive, we have a unstable node.

- Since $A$ is not diagonal and has a repeated eigenvalue, there is only one linearly independent eigenvector. So, we have a degenerate node.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/6f6a92e2b8fb89f833268a5526876cb3af5215db0193a2aaaad8aac5790752ea.svg)
where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *two independent eigenvectors*, then $A$ is the scalar matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/69199c6f84ebe1f9587b9207a3f1fc42c909fc9a1e43041e11fcab9ce881e5d1.svg)
In this case, every direction through the origin behaves like an eigenvector direction, and trajectories are straight lines:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{\lambda t} \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

So the phase portrait is a **star node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable star node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable star node**.

Let's see an example.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/6f6a92e2b8fb89f833268a5526876cb3af5215db0193a2aaaad8aac5790752ea.svg)
where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *two independent eigenvectors*, then $A$ is the scalar matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/69199c6f84ebe1f9587b9207a3f1fc42c909fc9a1e43041e11fcab9ce881e5d1.svg)
In this case, every direction through the origin behaves like an eigenvector direction, and trajectories are straight lines:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{\lambda t} \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

So the phase portrait is a **star node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable star node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable star node**.

Let's see an example.

tutorials.name: A Worked Example of a Star Node
tutorials.problem:
Let's sketch the phase portrait of the following linear system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/f58fb57caaba8c5f6a110c72565c24803ac233f41b8eb2db0c5221bcf12d7fe2.svg)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/65298928a44147868c82da753a731e35c3aa0ad5e4b3400819d9d9f16f546a34.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/694a89326f61bbbba7e91db5dcb607a74f99881ce16059450dbe1bbac7ee797e.svg)

The general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/abd4dbe3156abbcd645e670fb893f93cc8765cba4b1da9bde11075e211f1eeaa.svg)

Notice that for each vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/9df6cb20bf3163f53850730242138ec62412ccc8af23098130d71228cac4b82a.svg) we get the straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/7166c456c7912bf31d4ff2d98f4e4206537f8d01aca086fdba3c15b394db4b81.svg)
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/23074d10911b113811cc92bdc88a61a6758dbd8772c21425159c5e95d30b1075.svg)

Since $e^{2t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t \to \infty,$ so the origin is an unstable node.

The phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/b32b5666c0138f5c17ff1622cef9bca6fb019375f6748b6422c11a547cfad282.png)

tutorials.title: A Worked Example of a Star Node
tutorials.content:
Let's sketch the phase portrait of the following linear system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/f58fb57caaba8c5f6a110c72565c24803ac233f41b8eb2db0c5221bcf12d7fe2.svg)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/65298928a44147868c82da753a731e35c3aa0ad5e4b3400819d9d9f16f546a34.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/694a89326f61bbbba7e91db5dcb607a74f99881ce16059450dbe1bbac7ee797e.svg)

The general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/abd4dbe3156abbcd645e670fb893f93cc8765cba4b1da9bde11075e211f1eeaa.svg)

Notice that for each vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/9df6cb20bf3163f53850730242138ec62412ccc8af23098130d71228cac4b82a.svg) we get the straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/7166c456c7912bf31d4ff2d98f4e4206537f8d01aca086fdba3c15b394db4b81.svg)
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/23074d10911b113811cc92bdc88a61a6758dbd8772c21425159c5e95d30b1075.svg)

Since $e^{2t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t \to \infty,$ so the origin is an unstable node.

The phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/b32b5666c0138f5c17ff1622cef9bca6fb019375f6748b6422c11a547cfad282.png)

tutorials.name: Systems With Repeated Eigenvalues
tutorials.problem:
Recall that in this topic, we're studying phase portraits of linear systems
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/28d8900ae13325f715af9679fdeab6f26645e322ea0df016618826a5b3dee328.svg)
where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *only one eigenvector* $\mathbf{v},$ and if $\mathbf{w}$ is a generalized eigenvector satisfying

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v},
$$

then the general solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=c_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}+c_2 e^{\lambda t}\bigl(t\,\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\bigr).
$$

Here, the eigenvector line (the line through the origin parallel to $\mathbf{v}$) is still a straight-line solution, but other trajectories are *curved* and become tangent to that eigenvector line.

In cases like this, the phase portrait is a **degenerate node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable degenerate node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable degenerate node**.

Let's see an example.

tutorials.name: A Worked Example for a System With Repeated Eigenvalues
tutorials.problem:
Consider the following system of linear differential equations: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue of the system's matrix $A$ is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/23616d197363a3fd8ad4689a0b1e547c7b1044e0929cfd96add65a26e940731f.svg) The vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/3e434cc0b5ca5d288695abb58500e8f4ca6be0c0cf2ecb5200d03f5fbcf522c2.svg) is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ 

Let's sketch the phase portrait of the system.

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/0f7c56980abff1ad84ca69aa98730bca2988cf5430f181f69d191f1e3c28eff0.svg) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/c9d65d3792c7cced40b86834fbd66769daa714ed58ffcde025cb956763c2c670.svg)
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move toward infinity in the phase plane as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/98fc60d566b520f3d943e42ee8f4e07aa0bdd33b53fbb04981c2e8f4001210fd.png)

When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{t} \\ y={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.title: A Worked Example for a System With Repeated Eigenvalues
tutorials.content:
Consider the following system of linear differential equations: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue of the system's matrix $A$ is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/23616d197363a3fd8ad4689a0b1e547c7b1044e0929cfd96add65a26e940731f.svg) The vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/3e434cc0b5ca5d288695abb58500e8f4ca6be0c0cf2ecb5200d03f5fbcf522c2.svg) is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ 

Let's sketch the phase portrait of the system.

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/0f7c56980abff1ad84ca69aa98730bca2988cf5430f181f69d191f1e3c28eff0.svg) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/c9d65d3792c7cced40b86834fbd66769daa714ed58ffcde025cb956763c2c670.svg)
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move toward infinity in the phase plane as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/98fc60d566b520f3d943e42ee8f4e07aa0bdd33b53fbb04981c2e8f4001210fd.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/6170eec4537e26afef2a794426b4f5231b0f4366c21b8860c332f1ec7573b96a.svg)
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{t} \\ y={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $1.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.30$ | $0$ | $3.98$ |
| $y$ | $0.61$ | $1$ | $3.32$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/4fbc1650377d580d7129701d745dc8cad89d2d1d061b8f6dca8127f0ce062dc8.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14124655/assets/499391b5bc015bd96bbe85d72e3937e87a5e89081951aaad0a752582cb87f15f.png)

Introduction

Systems With Repeated Eigenvalues
?

If has only one eigenvector and if is a generalized eigenvector satisfying then the general solution takes the form Here, the eigenvector line (the line through the origin parallel to ) is still a straight-line solution, but other trajectories are curved and become tangent to that eigenvector line.

In cases like this, the phase portrait is a degenerate node:

  • If trajectories move away from the origin and we have an unstable degenerate node.

  • If trajectories move toward the origin and we have a stable degenerate node.
